title: Django and DRF in one lesson

story: RH-1234 asks for a "No projects yet" card when a workgroup has no projects. In the browser's network tab you can see the page call GET /api/v2/projects/ and get back an empty list. Before you trust that empty list, you want to read the code that produces it, so you search fcp's backend the way you would search a Next.js app for app/api/projects/route.ts.

There is no such file. The only line that mentions projects/ is router.register(f"{API_PREFIX}projects", ProjectViewSetRhino, basename="project"), and the class it names has no method called get. Yet the endpoint lists, creates, renames and deletes projects, and Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, will need to change it and test it.
hook.question: How does one router.register line become a whole JSON API, and how do you test that API without starting a server?

read.h: Four parts, and a model first
p: fcp's cloud service is a Django project with Django REST Framework (DRF) on top. Django is the web framework: it owns the database, the URLs and the settings. DRF adds what a JSON API needs. Four parts work together on every request, and each one has a TypeScript cousin you already know. The model is the table, much like a Prisma model. The serializer checks incoming JSON and shapes outgoing JSON, like a zod schema with a toJSON. The viewset is a class with one method per action, like a route handler. The router builds the URL patterns from the viewset, like file-based routing does from your folders.

Start with the model. A model is a class whose fields describe the columns of a table, and Django's ORM (object-relational mapper, the layer that writes SQL for you) turns Project.objects.filter(workgroup="wg-rhino") into a SELECT. You never change the table by hand. You change the model and run makemigrations, which compares the models with the last migration and writes the next migration file: a numbered Python file that describes one change to the schema. migrate applies it to a database. Migrations are committed with the code, and fcp's CI fails when a model changed but nobody wrote its migration.

code.text:
from django.db import models


class Project(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    workgroup = models.CharField(max_length=60)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

notes.text: A model is a class that inherits from models.Model. Django adds an id primary key by itself.
Each field is one column. CharField with max_length becomes varchar(120).
auto_now_add fills the time when the row is created; the client never sends it.

read.see:
$ uv run python manage.py makemigrations projects
Migrations for 'projects':
  projects/migrations/0001_initial.py
    + Create model Project
$ uv run python manage.py sqlmigrate projects 0001
CREATE TABLE "projects_project" ("id" integer NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, "name" varchar(120) NOT NULL, "workgroup" varchar(60) NOT NULL, "created_at" datetime NOT NULL);

p: A serializer works in both directions. On the way in, it takes the JSON body, checks every field and turns it into Python values; on the way out, it turns a model object into JSON. A ModelSerializer reads the field types from the model, so you only list which fields the API exposes and which ones the client may not write. When the body is wrong, nothing is saved: the viewset answers 400 with a dictionary of field errors, for example {"name": ["This field may not be blank."]}.

This is why the serializer, not the model, is where an API's rules live. Code that writes rows straight into the database skips every one of these checks, which matters later for test data: data created through the API has passed the same door that real users pass.

code.text:
from rest_framework import serializers

from .models import Project


class ProjectSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Project
        fields = ["id", "name", "workgroup", "created_at"]
        read_only_fields = ["id", "created_at"]

notes.text: ModelSerializer builds one serializer field per model field, with the same types and limits.
Meta is an inner class that holds the settings; DRF and Django use this pattern everywhere.
The fields the API shows. A field missing here is invisible to clients.
Shown in responses, ignored in request bodies.

read.h: The viewset and the router write the routes
p: Now the mystery from the story. A ModelViewSet already has a method for each of the six actions: list, retrieve, create, update, partial_update and destroy. You give it a serializer and a get_queryset method, the query that decides which rows this request may see, and it does the rest. The router then turns one register call into two URL patterns: projects/ for list (GET) and create (POST), and projects/<pk>/ for retrieve, update, partial update and delete (GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE).

So when you read an fcp endpoint, you look in three places. Which viewset does the router register? Which serializer does get_serializer_class return? And what does get_queryset filter? In fcp's projects viewset the answers are ProjectViewSetRhino, ProjectFlatSerializer and the projects this user may see, and the empty list in RH-1234 comes from that query finding no rows for the workgroup.

code.text:
from rest_framework import viewsets

from .models import Project
from .serializers import ProjectSerializer


class ProjectViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = ProjectSerializer

    def get_queryset(self):
        projects = Project.objects.order_by("-created_at")
        workgroup = self.request.query_params.get("workgroup")
        return projects.filter(workgroup=workgroup) if workgroup else projects


# mysite/urls.py
from django.urls import include, path
from rest_framework.routers import SimpleRouter

from projects.views import ProjectViewSet

router = SimpleRouter()
router.register("projects", ProjectViewSet, basename="project")

urlpatterns = [path("api/", include(router.urls))]

notes.text: ModelViewSet brings all six actions. fcp's viewsets combine smaller mixins to pick only some of them.
Called on every request. self.request is the incoming request, so the query can depend on the user or a filter.
One line, two URL patterns. basename names them project-list and project-detail.

read.see:
$ uv run python manage.py shell -c "from mysite.urls import router; [print(u.pattern, u.name) for u in router.urls]"
^projects/$ project-list
^projects/(?P<pk>[^/.]+)/$ project-detail

read.h: Testing without a server: APIClient and a throwaway database
p: You do not need a running server or a network to test an endpoint. DRF's APIClient sends a request straight into Django inside the test process: client.post("/api/projects/", data, format="json") runs the router, the viewset, the serializer and the model, and gives you a response with status_code and .json(). It is closer to calling your Next.js handler with a fake Request than to opening a browser.

The plugin pytest-django connects Django to pytest. Before the tests start, it creates a separate test database and runs every migration into it, so your real database is never touched. A test may use the database only if it carries the django_db marker; without it, pytest-django stops the test with an error, which keeps slow database tests visible. Each marked test runs inside a database transaction that is rolled back at the end, so every test starts with empty tables, and the test that creates a project never leaks it into the test that expects an empty list.

notes.text: pytestmark applies the marker to every test in the file: all of them may use the test database.
A fixture, as in the previous lesson. Each test gets its own client.
The second argument becomes the query string, ?workgroup=wg-empty.
format="json" sends a JSON body, like fetch with Content-Type: application/json.
The exact error a client would see, so the test checks the API's contract, not internals.

read.see:
$ uv run pytest -v
tests/test_projects_api.py::test_a_new_workgroup_has_no_projects PASSED  [ 33%]
tests/test_projects_api.py::test_create_a_project PASSED                 [ 66%]
tests/test_projects_api.py::test_a_project_needs_a_name PASSED           [100%]
============================== 3 passed in 0.20s ===============================

p: fcp's cloud has more than 200 migrations, and running all of them for every test run, on every parallel worker, takes minutes. Postgres can copy a whole database quickly with CREATE DATABASE new_db TEMPLATE old_db. So the planned API test layer replaces pytest-django's database setup with a session-scoped fixture: one worker runs the migrations once into a template database, and every worker then gets its own copy of it in seconds.

The template's name includes a hash of the migration file names, so adding a migration builds a fresh template automatically. SQLite, which the lab uses, has no templates, which is one reason a real Postgres is used for fcp's tests.

lab.title: A projects API in Django and DRF
lab.goal: Build a small projects API with a model, a serializer, a viewset and a router, and test it in-process with APIClient and pytest-django.

guess.q: The viewset has no get method, and the router has one line: router.register("projects", ProjectViewSet, basename="project"). Which requests work?

options.text: Only GET /api/projects/, because the router registers one URL per register call.
options.why: The router makes two URL patterns, one for the collection and one for a single item, and each accepts several methods.

options.text: None, until you write a get, post, put and delete method on the viewset.
options.why: That would be a plain APIView. A ModelViewSet already contains the six actions.

options.text: GET and POST on /api/projects/, and GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE on /api/projects/<id>/.
options.why: ModelViewSet has list, create, retrieve, update, partial_update and destroy, and the router maps them to those methods and two URLs.

Write the four files from the Understand step: the model, the serializer, the viewset and the URLs.

cat > projects/serializers.py <<'EOF'

cat > projects/views.py <<'EOF'
from rest_framework import viewsets

from .models import Project
from .serializers import ProjectSerializer


class ProjectViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):

    def get_queryset(self):
        projects = Project.objects.order_by("-created_at")

EOF
cat > mysite/urls.py <<'EOF'

from rest_framework.routers import SimpleRouter

from projects.views import ProjectViewSet

router = SimpleRouter()

EOF

follow.say: Run them on two workers. Each worker gets its own test database, so the tests cannot see each other's rows.
Last, add the file for the Fix it step. Do not read it closely yet.
follow.do:
cat > tests/test_fix.py <<'EOF'
from rest_framework.test import APIClient


def test_list_projects_of_a_workgroup():
    client = APIClient()
    client.post("/api/projects/", {"name": "Lung CT", "workgroup": "wg-rhino"}, format="json")
    response = client.get("/api/projects/", {"workgroup": "wg-rhino"})
    assert [p["name"] for p in response.json()] == ["Lung CT"]
EOF

lab.build: Projects can now be archived. Add archived = models.BooleanField(default=False) to the model, add "archived" to the serializer's fields, and make get_queryset hide archived projects. Write test_an_archived_project_leaves_the_list: create a project through the API, PATCH /api/projects/<id>/ with {"archived": true}, and check that the workgroup's list is empty. Run the tests before you create the migration and read the error, then run makemigrations and run them again. Finish with uv run python manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run, the check fcp's CI runs.
checks: makemigrations wrote projects/migrations/0001_initial.py, and sqlmigrate printed a CREATE TABLE.
The router printed two patterns: project-list and project-detail.
uv run pytest -v shows 3 passed, and uv run pytest -n 2 -q passes too.
Before the new migration, the archived tests failed with no such column: projects_project.archived.
After makemigrations, all tests pass, and makemigrations --check --dry-run prints No changes detected.

solution.text:
# projects/models.py: one new field
    archived = models.BooleanField(default=False)

# projects/serializers.py: expose it
        fields = ["id", "name", "workgroup", "created_at", "archived"]

# projects/views.py: hide archived projects
        projects = Project.objects.filter(archived=False).order_by("-created_at")

# tests/test_projects_api.py
def test_an_archived_project_leaves_the_list(client):
    created = client.post("/api/projects/", {"name": "Lung CT", "workgroup": "wg-rhino"}, format="json").json()
    response = client.patch(f"/api/projects/{created['id']}/", {"archived": True}, format="json")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert client.get("/api/projects/", {"workgroup": "wg-rhino"}).json() == []

# then, in the terminal
# uv run python manage.py makemigrations projects

lab.fix: tests/test_fix.py creates a project and lists the workgroup's projects, but uv run pytest -q tests/test_fix.py fails with RuntimeError: Database access not allowed. The test looks correct. Find what every test in test_projects_api.py has that this one does not, add it, and run the file again.
explain: A POST to /api/projects/ with an empty name returns 400 and saves nothing. Which of the four parts made that decision, and how?
Why does test_a_new_workgroup_has_no_projects see an empty list even though test_create_a_project created a project?
The tests failed before you wrote the migration for archived. Why does a missing migration break the tests and not only production?
lab.done: All tests pass, including your archived test and the repaired test_fix.py, and makemigrations --check --dry-run prints No changes detected.

check.q: A client sends POST /api/projects/ with {"name": ""}. Where is the request rejected, and what does the client get?

options.text: In the database, which raises an IntegrityError that becomes a 500.
options.why: The request never reaches the database. The serializer checks the body first.

options.text: In the serializer, which finds the blank name, so the viewset answers 400 with the field errors.
options.why: is_valid() fails, nothing is saved, and the client gets {"name": ["This field may not be blank."]}.

options.text: In the router, which only accepts bodies that match the model.
options.why: The router only maps URLs and methods to viewset actions. It never looks at the body.

check.q: You add a field to a Django model and run the tests without running makemigrations. What happens?

options.text: The tests that touch the table fail, because the test database is built from the migrations, which do not have the new column.
options.why: pytest-django builds the test database by running every migration, so the model and the table disagree. fcp's CI also fails on makemigrations --check.

options.text: Django adds the column to the test database automatically, so the tests pass.
options.why: Django only changes tables through migrations. Without one, the column does not exist.

options.text: Nothing changes until you deploy, because migrations only matter in production.
options.why: Every database, including the test database, is built from migrations.

check.q: Test A creates a project, and test B, which runs after A, checks that the list is empty. Both carry django_db. Why does B pass?

options.text: pytest runs each test in a different database file.
options.why: Without xdist, all tests share one test database. The isolation comes from transactions.

options.text: APIClient deletes every row it created when the test ends.
options.why: APIClient only sends requests. It does not track or delete what they created.

options.text: Each test runs inside a transaction that pytest-django rolls back at the end, so A's row is gone before B starts.
options.why: That is why every test starts with empty tables and tests can run in any order.

p: Every fcp endpoint follows this shape. rhinoCore/urls.py registers each viewset with a router under /api/v1/ and /api/v2/, fcp's viewsets combine mixins to pick their actions, and the serializers decide what clients see. drf-spectacular reads the same serializers and viewsets to generate the OpenAPI schema, which the breaking-change check in a later lesson compares between main and a pull request.

The planned API test layer, tests_api, tests endpoints exactly as this lab does: pytest-django, an in-process client, a template database copied per xdist worker, and test data created through the API with a real login token, so the serializers and permissions are part of every test.

tickets.why: tests_api with pytest-django, a first APIClient test and the template-database fixture from the Go deeper panel.
Runs the API layer as its own CI job with a throwaway Postgres service.
Data builders that create workgroups, users and projects through the API instead of writing rows.
Ports the first cloud-only integration tests into tests_api, asserting on responses the way this lab does.

words.plain: A Django class whose fields are a table's columns; the ORM turns its methods into SQL.
A committed, numbered file with one schema change; makemigrations writes it and migrate applies it.
DRF's validator and converter between JSON and Python objects, like a zod schema with a toJSON.
A class with one method per action (list, create, retrieve, update, destroy) for one kind of object.
Turns a registered viewset into URL patterns, so nobody writes the route table by hand.
DRF's test client: sends a request into Django inside the test process, with no server or network.

review.q: Someone asks where the code for PATCH /api/v2/projects/<uid>/ lives in fcp. Which three things do you look up, in which files?
review.a: The router.register line in rhinoCore/urls.py (which viewset), the viewset's get_serializer_class and get_queryset (which serializer, which rows), and the serializer's fields (what may change).

review.q: Write a pytest-django test that checks GET /api/projects/?workgroup=wg-empty returns an empty list.
review.a: Mark it with django_db, create an APIClient (usually through a fixture), call client.get("/api/projects/", {"workgroup": "wg-empty"}), assert status_code == 200 and response.json() == [].

review.q: Why should test data be created through the API rather than written straight into tables?
review.a: Data written straight into tables skips the serializer's checks and the permissions, so tests can pass on data no real user could create.

remember: A request goes router, viewset, serializer, model; APIClient sends one through all four inside the test, against a database that is fresh for every test.
